structure.overview: The case concerns Afghan nationals (Applicants) who received Facilitation Letters intended to help them pass Taliban checkpoints and allegedly promised Temporary Resident Permits (TRPs) to enter Canada. The Applicants claim these letters were issued under the Crown prerogative and that their rights under the Charter were engaged, seeking mandamus relief. The Federal Court rejected the Applicants' claims, finding no Crown prerogative authority or promise of visas, dismissed the Charter claim, and certified three questions of general importance for appeal.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Respondents issued Facilitation Letters in 2021 to help designated Afghan nationals pass Taliban checkpoints to reach Kabul Airport.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants claim the Facilitation Letters promised them TRPs to enter Canada under the Crown prerogative, despite no visa applications or issuances.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In August 2021, GAC issued Facilitation Letters to help Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and families pass checkpoints to Kabul Airport.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The GAC Facilitation Letter stated that named persons were Canadian citizens granted visas to enter Canada and requested safe passage to Kabul Airport.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: IRCC used the Facilitation Letters from August 19 to 30, 2021, to help Afghan nationals with immigration applications reach evacuation flights.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: On August 28, 2021, IRCC declared the Facilitation Letters invalid for boarding flights to Canada, limiting their purpose to checkpoint passage only.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: IRCC repeated the invalidation message of the Facilitation Letters on August 30 and October 6, 2021.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Mr. Young received and modified the Facilitation Letter template to remove Canadian citizen references, then sent it to Senator McPhedran and Ms. Robinson.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Ms. Robinson distributed personalized Facilitation Letters to at-risk individuals, including the Applicants, via various organizations.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicants received their Facilitation Letters from FIFA between August 29 and September 7, 2021, after IRCC's invalidation message.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court's jurisdiction for mandamus is under Federal Courts Act s.18(1) and IRPA s.72; mandamus is an extraordinary remedy assessed case-by-case.

citations.cite: Federal Courts Act, RSC, 1985, c F-7, s 18(1)
citations.why: Court's jurisdiction for mandamus

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, s 72
citations.why: Mandamus recognized under IRPA

citations.cite: Tapie v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 1048 at para 7
citations.why: Mandamus is an extraordinary remedy

citations.cite: Oladele v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1161 at para 28
citations.why: Mandamus remedy assessment

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The mandamus test requires a public legal duty owed to the applicant, a clear right, no other remedy, practical effect, no equitable bar, and balance of convenience.

citations.cite: Apotex v Canada (Attorney General), 1993 CanLII 3004 (FCA), [1994] 1 FC 742 (FCA)
citations.why: Mandamus test criteria

citations.cite: Sharafaldin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 768 at para 34
citations.why: Recent summary of mandamus test

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicants were not intended recipients of Facilitation Letters, received them after evacuation flights ended and after IRCC invalidated them.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants define Crown prerogative as discretionary authority legally left to the Crown, a limited non-statutory administrative power.

citations.cite: Canada (Prime Minister) v Khadr, 2010 SCC 3 at para 34
citations.why: Definition of Crown prerogative

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants assert three Crown prerogatives apply: foreign affairs, admission/exclusion of aliens, and war and peace including military.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants say the foreign affairs prerogative includes consular functions like issuing visas, citing the Vienna Convention and related Act.

citations.cite: Vienna Convention on Consular Relations
citations.why: Defines consular functions including issuing visas

citations.cite: Foreign Missions and International Organizations Act, SC 1991, c 41
citations.why: Incorporates Vienna Convention into domestic law

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants argue the admission/exclusion prerogative is a derivative of foreign affairs prerogative, citing cases recognizing it.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Obodzinsky (TD), 2002 FCT 943 at paras 49-54
citations.why: Supports admission/exclusion prerogative

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Kisluk, 1999 CanLII 8351 (FC) at para 164
citations.why: Supports admission/exclusion prerogative

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants say the war and peace prerogative, recognized in Operation Dismantle, authorizes military deployments like the 2021 Afghanistan evacuation.

citations.cite: Canada v Operation Dismantle Inc., 1983 CanLII 4977 (FCA) at 779 (aff’d 1985 CanLII 74 (SCC))
citations.why: Recognizes war and peace prerogative

citations.cite: Department of National Defence, The Crown Prerogative as applied to Military Operations, March 2020
citations.why: Explains legal authority from Crown prerogative for military operations

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants argue IRPA s.24 has not extinguished the Crown prerogative to issue visas, citing Khadr and DND's position on prerogative powers.

citations.cite: Khadr, para 35
citations.why: Section 10 of DFAIT Act did not extinguish foreign affairs prerogative

citations.cite: National Defence Act, RSC, 1985, c N-5, ss 31(1) and 33(1)
citations.why: DND says these do not extinguish prerogative to deploy CAF

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court respectfully disagrees with the Applicants' arguments regarding the Crown prerogative.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Parliament's IRPA governs entry to Canada; visa decisions must comply with IRPA and its regulations, respecting the rule of law.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Supreme Court in Khadr stated that statutory provisions can limit or set aside the Crown prerogative.

citations.cite: Khadr
citations.why: Statutory provisions can limit Crown prerogative

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Parliament's IRPA requires foreign nationals to apply for visas and officers to issue them after examination, limiting prerogative.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, s 11(1)
citations.why: Statutory visa application and issuance requirements

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Only the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration may designate officers under IRPA to carry out its purposes, per section 6.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, s 6
citations.why: Minister's exclusive authority to designate officers

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Finding Facilitation Letters issued under Crown prerogative would undermine Parliamentary sovereignty and allow executive to bypass laws.

citations.cite: Reference re Pan-Canadian Securities Regulation, 2018 SCC 48 at para 54
citations.why: Parliamentary sovereignty means legislature's power is supreme

citations.cite: Ross River Dena Council Band v Canada, 2002 SCC 54 at para 4
citations.why: Crown cannot disregard statutory limitations and rely on prerogative

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court rejects the Applicants' Crown prerogative arguments as inconsistent with Parliamentary sovereignty.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The prerogative is discretionary authority legally left to the Crown, a limited non-statutory administrative power.

citations.cite: Reference as to the Effect of the Exercise of the Royal Prerogative of Mercy Upon Deportation Proceedings, [1933] S.C.R. 269, p. 272
citations.why: Definition of prerogative power

citations.cite: A. V. Dicey, Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (8th ed. 1915), p. 420
citations.why: Definition of prerogative power

citations.cite: Hogg, at p. 1-17
citations.why: Definition of prerogative power

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Minister Sajjan testified he knew Facilitation Letters were used but did not authorize or know about their dissemination.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Young was not authorized by the Ministers to grant visas or authorize Ms. Robinson to distribute Facilitation Letters.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Under IRPA s.6, delegation must be in writing specifying powers; no such delegation authorized issuing Facilitation Letters here.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, s 6(1)
citations.why: Delegation must be in writing specifying powers and duties

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The IRPA does not allow sub-delegation, reflecting the general administrative law presumption against it, as explained in Morton v Canada.

citations.cite: Morton v Canada (Fisheries and Oceans), 2015 FC 575 at para 79
citations.why: Defines sub-delegation and supports presumption against it

citations.cite: Robert W. Macaulay and James L.H. Sprague, Practice and Procedure before Administrative Tribunals (loose-leaf) (Toronto: Carswell, 1988) (2012 updated) at 5-20
citations.why: Provides definition of sub-delegation

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sub-delegation is only allowed when the action is purely administrative without significant discretion, as per Morton.

citations.cite: Morton v Canada (Fisheries and Oceans), 2015 FC 575 at para 80
citations.why: Sets exception to presumption against sub-delegation for purely administrative acts

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Ms. Robinson could not have been sub-delegated authority to add names or issue visas, as this is not a purely administrative act.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The situation reflects a poor understanding of Facilitation Letters and Canadian immigration by Mr. Young, Senator McPhedran, Ms. Robinson, and third parties.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicants' claim that Ms. Robinson was delegated authority to act for IRCC is rejected.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Public law promissory estoppel requires a clear promise by a public authority inducing reliance, similar to private law estoppel.

citations.cite: Immeubles Jacques Robitaille inc v Québec (City), 2014 SCC 34 at para 19
citations.why: Defines public law promissory estoppel requirements

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Supreme Court noted significant differences between private and public law promissory estoppel.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Public law promissory estoppel does not apply here as no promise was made by Canadian officials and estoppel cannot grant unauthorized powers.

citations.cite: Tapambwa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FCA 34 at para 67
citations.why: Estoppel cannot give powers not legally possessed

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Even if a promise existed, enforcing it would override IRPA provisions, undermining Parliamentary sovereignty and rule of law.
idea_list: promise unenforceable as it overrides IRPA
would violate Parliamentary sovereignty and rule of law

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Accepting Facilitation Letters as visas would violate Parliamentary sovereignty and the rule of law.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds no visa promise was made, which disposes of the Charter claim, but will still assess the Applicants' arguments.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants argue their nexus to Canada arises from state actions involving Facilitation Letters and delegation occurring in Canadian government offices.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants claim their situation is like refugee claimants, citing Singh for section 7 Charter rights outside Canada with well-founded fear of persecution.

citations.cite: Singh v Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 SCR 177
citations.why: Applicants rely on Singh for Charter rights outside Canada

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees Charter does not apply to risks from foreign entities, only to Canadian state actions, citing relevant cases.
idea_list: Charter does not apply to foreign risks
Charter applies to Canadian extraterritorial actions only

citations.cite: Charter, section 32
citations.why: Limits Charter application to government actors

citations.cite: Dickson v Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation, 2024 SCC 10 at para 69
citations.why: Supports Charter's limited application

citations.cite: Khadr at para 14
citations.why: Charter applies to Canadian participation in foreign acts violating rights

citations.cite: R v Hape, 2007 SCC 26 at para 52
citations.why: Same as above

citations.cite: Canada (Justice) v Khadr, 2008 SCC 28 at para 19
citations.why: Same as above

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicants lack a nexus to Canada and thus cannot claim Charter protection, supported by multiple Federal Court decisions.

citations.cite: Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act (CA) (Re), 2022 FC 1444 at paras 170-171
citations.why: Supports lack of nexus to Canada

citations.cite: Slahi v Canada (Justice), 2009 FC 160 at paras 47-48, 52
citations.why: Supports lack of nexus to Canada

citations.cite: Slahi v Canada (Justice), 2009 FCA 259
citations.why: Affirms above

citations.cite: Toronto Coalition to Stop the War v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2010 FC 957 at para 81
citations.why: Supports lack of nexus to Canada

citations.cite: Zeng v Canada (Attorney General), 2013 FC 104 at paras 70-72
citations.why: Supports lack of nexus to Canada

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Crown prerogative is not engaged as the government did not issue Facilitation Letters or affect Applicants' risk; letters came from unauthorized third parties.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicants' hardship in Afghanistan lacks causal link to Canadian state action; government inaction alone cannot ground a section 7 Charter claim.
idea_list: no causal link to Canadian state action
government inaction insufficient for Charter claim

citations.cite: Canada v Boloh 1(a), 2023 FCA 120 at paras 44, 47-48
citations.why: Government inaction alone insufficient for Charter claim

citations.cite: Gosselin v Québec (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 84 at paras 75, 77, 81-84
citations.why: Same as above

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicants' Charter claim fails.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondents argue DND and GAC lack authority under immigration law, so decisions here are not under IRPA.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondents contend Crown prerogative decisions fall outside IRPA section 72 and must proceed under Federal Courts Act section 18.1, granting automatic appeal rights.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects Respondents' position and agrees to assess if proposed questions meet certification requirements.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: IRPA paragraph 74(d) limits appeals to certified questions of general importance transcending party interests, per Supreme Court and FCA precedents.
idea_list: IRPA limits appeals to certified questions

citations.cite: Mason v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 at para 37
citations.why: Defines certification requirements for appeal

citations.cite: Lunyamila v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2018 FCA 22 at para 46
citations.why: Supports certification criteria

citations.cite: Lewis v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 FCA 130 at para 36
citations.why: Supports certification criteria

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Both parties proposed several questions for certification before the hearing.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The court requested additional submissions on certification requirements and impact of factual findings on certification.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Parties could not agree on certified questions and each proposed their own serious questions of general importance.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants propose five certification questions about Crown prerogative, delegation, Facilitation Letters, promissory estoppel, and Charter application.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondents propose eight certification questions grouped into Crown prerogative, public law promissory estoppel, and Charter application categories.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Certification questions depend on factual findings that Mr. Young was authorized under Crown prerogative to issue and delegate Facilitation Letters.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The evidence does not support that Mr. Young was authorized under Crown prerogative to issue or delegate Facilitation Letters.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Despite findings, the court certifies three questions on Crown prerogative authority and judicial review under IRPA, considering case uniqueness and possible error.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the three questions raised are broadly significant, involving federal prerogative authority and judicial review, and certifies them for appeal.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court decides not to award costs.
